subtype: Approach: time-boxed learning sprint with a deliverable [Action]
passage: I watched Samir do it last month, so let me write down what I saw, Bhupen here. He said he was going to learn a new tool by shipping a small app in seven days. Two hours a day, after dinner, no more. He wrote a list on the fridge: day 1 setup, day 2 screens, day 3 saving data. He told me he would show me the result on Saturday, and that I was to say "not good enough" if it was not working. I do not know if he was nervous. I saw him at the table every night with the same mug. On Saturday the app was small and wobbly, and it ran. He grinned. I clapped. Then he asked what to fix next.

qa.q: How many days did Samir give himself to build the app?
What might Samir have felt on the day of the demo, according to what Bhupen saw?
qa.a: Samir probably felt proud and relieved, since he grinned when the small wobbly app ran, though Bhupen admits not knowing if Samir was nervous.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Samir use if a day goes badly, and why?
qa.a: Samir could move the demo by a day or cut a screen, because the time limit is a tool and the deliverable matters more than the exact deadline.

qa.q: What is it like for Bhupen to watch Samir without knowing what he feels?
qa.a: Bhupen sees the mug and the fridge list but not the feelings, so Bhupen only reports what was seen and the grin on Saturday.

grounding: Shows a week-long learning sprint with a modest daily time limit and a demo to a friend as a commitment.

subtype: Approach: time-boxed learning sprint with a deliverable [Action]
passage:
Day 1, Saturday. Aditi writes on a sticky note: 'Seven days. Two hours a day. A working to-do app with a backend. Demo to Santosh, Friday, 8 p.m.' Santosh replies to her message: 'I'm bringing samosas. No excuses 👍'
Day 4, Tuesday. Her two hours are up at 10 p.m. and the save button still throws an error. She wants to keep going till two. Instead she writes the error on the sticky note, so tomorrow starts with it, and closes the laptop.
Day 7, Friday. At 7:45 the app adds, ticks and deletes tasks, though editing a task is still broken. Santosh arrives with samosas and types 'buy milk'. It saves. Aditi laughs, a little shakily, and shows him the list of what she learned this week, one line per evening.

qa.q: What time was the demo to Santosh set for?
Why did Aditi stop at 10 p.m. on Tuesday with the error still there, and how was she feeling?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and tempted to keep going till two, but she trusted the two-hour limit and wrote the error down so the next session started with it.

qa.q: What would you change first if the app had been far from working by day 6?
qa.a: Cut it down to the core, such as adding and ticking tasks, so something still runs for the Friday demo.

qa.q: How does the demo feel to Santosh?
qa.a: For Santosh it is a fun evening and proof the promise was kept; typing 'buy milk' and seeing it save makes the week's work real.

grounding: Shows a student giving themselves seven days at two hours a day to build a small app, with a Friday demo to a friend keeping them committed.

subtype: Approach: time-boxed learning sprint with a deliverable [Action]
passage:
Keerthana, you think learning a new thing fast is a new problem? Sit. When I was about your age, in Coimbatore, our college got its first computers, and the professor said anyone who could make a working program by month-end could join his project.
My classmates planned to learn properly first. I, Sudha, was lazier and more scared, so I made a deal with my friend Revathi. Seven days, two hours after dinner, and on Sunday I would show her a program that added up the hostel mess bills. If I showed nothing, I would wash her plates for a week.
Every night: the manual, two hours, then stop. On day five it printed rubbish and I nearly gave up. On Sunday it worked, only for four students, but it worked. Revathi was almost disappointed about the plates. The professor took me on.

qa.q: What did Sudha's program add up?
Why did Sudha make the deal with Revathi, and what was Sudha feeling then?
qa.a: Sudha felt scared and admits to being lazier than the classmates, so a promised demo with a forfeit gave the push needed to start.

qa.q: What choice on day five kept the plan alive?
qa.a: When it printed rubbish, Sudha nearly gave up but kept to the two hours a night, so the Sunday deadline still held.

qa.q: How did the deal look to Revathi?
qa.a: Revathi became the judge of the commitment and was almost disappointed to lose the plate-washing prize when the program worked.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a seven-day, two-hours-a-night plan to build a working program, with a demo to a friend and a forfeit keeping the commitment.
